Defense of the Ancients. Currently running Dota (Wc3 mod), Dota 2 (Valve) and Dota 2 Reborn Beta (Valve) with 10m+ players playing Dota 2 alone. Icefrog keeps the Wc3 mod as close to Dota 2 as possible, though the engine gets in his way occasionally. He is very creative at making things work though.

The new Dota 2 Reborn utilises the new Source 2 engine, which is just beautiful. Able to run in 64bit now the game loads in no time. Sound is clearer, the whole game is crisper and can run at higher fps on older machines that Dota 2 can.

Dota 2 became popular around 2003, which is when (I'm pretty sure) Icefrog took over as main dev from Guinsoo who had taken it over from someone else before that. Icefrog, rumoured to be the stream personality 'Bruno', is quite possibly a game balancing legend. The current version is ridiculously balanced. The changes have made for a more active game, rewarding teamwork and coordination more than older versions which encouraged 4 protect 1 farming strats, snowballing and 5 man pushes.

Unlike LoL it is very, very skill rewarding. There are hundreds (thousands?) of little nuances to learn and adjust to. Thousands of spell/item interactions and combinations. Many heroes can be played 3, 4 or even 5 different ways and still have an impact on the outcome of the game. Some of these nuances turn players off the game because it's hard. Yeah, it might be difficult to get into but once you break that barrier you feel like a god.

The learning curve is steep, with over 100 heroes available to play from the word go. The reward matches it though. Amazing shit can be done by any hero in the right hands.

These kinds of questions are really the 'in the eye of the beholder' kind. What may be fun to some may feel archaic to others as certain features and mechanics have become standard over the years. That said, as someone with an older laptop and no real money to spend on the latest games, I'm required to find joy in what I currently have and what I know will run well for me. That said, here's my list:

Starsiege: Tribes. Still graphically advanced? Hell no. The community puts together nice looking configs every few months with better textures, but it's still very much a late-90s FPS. Try it out later into the evenings (usually after 6pm EST or so). - http://www.moddb.com/groups/fps-z-fanatics/downloads/tribes-2015

Legions: Overdrive. This game is pretty similar to Tribes, but also has a few unique elements that aren't in any Tribes game. It technically came out in 2008, though was re-launched in 2010. We usually get together on Saturdays around 8pm EST for some organized games, though you might get lucky and find a few populated games later at night during the week. - http://www.legionsoverdrive.com/

Day of Defeat: Source. A bit more of a traditional FPS compared to the previous two. No jetpacks or skiing or anything like that. I think it came out in 2007 or so, and is still populated enough to find a few games any time of the day pretty much. - http://www.dayofdefeat.com/

Chapter 3 opens with hooks describing her experience in an all-female and then a mixed-sex college. In the mixed-sex university (Stanford), she saw that women spoke up less than at the all-female college. The professors reinforced the idea in the women that they would never be as great thinkers or writers as the men.

At Stanford she met other feminist thinkers, and they passed out feminist poems in class and published feminist literature. They worked on a foundation of solidarity between women, "sisterhood". This required rooting out internalized sexism. This is when women see themselves as inferior to men and "compete with each other for patriarchal approval."

Sisterhood is pretty much just like the already accepted concept of male bonding. Men in groups support one another and work as a team. Within patriarchy, women can't do this. The purpose of sisterhood isn't to work against men, but to work for women.

The biggest issue that the feminist movement tackled in the 60s and 70s was women's control of their own sexuality. Birth control, freedom from rape and harassment, control of reproduction. Also important was job discrimination.

She's a pretty big proponent of sisterhood, or female solidarity. In her opinion, sisterhood always undermines patriarchy. It tends to fight against racism and classism, because women must bond across these divides.

There were challenges to female solidarity. Some women re-aligned themselves with sexist men, and some radical women felt betrayed by the movement. Hooks attributes this to complacency coming from fast gains for women's equality. This complacency led women to take feminist progress for granted, and so they didn't feel a need for female solidarity. This complacency continues today, with some young women having no knowledge of feminism, and thinking that sexism is over. This shows the need for continued feminist education. It's a work in progress, but feminist groups are making female solidarity a political reality.

Chapter 4

"Everything we do in life is rooted in theory." This is why new models for social interaction are needed. The primary goal of early feminist theory was explaining to men and women how sexist thinking worked and how we could challenge and change it. We are socialized to accept sexist thinking, and we need to consciously change this.

Feminist publishers were founded, and rediscovered forgotten or ignored work by women. Biases in education were exposed. One thing that feminist publishers and educators didn't do was trash works by men. The point of critiquing all-male canons of scholarship was to expose the bias and recover works by women, not to trash men. One example of this is the Nobel prize winning writer Toni Morrison, who was not widely read until feminists started writing about her works and bringing her works up in academia.

Women's studies programs became part of many universities. "Simply being the victim of an exploitative or oppressive system and even resisting it does not mean we understand why it's in place or how to change it. That's why the academic institution of feminism is important.

Feminism developed throughout the 70s, with black women and other women of color raising racial biases as a factor shaping feminist thought. There was resistance to this, as many privileged women thought that their experiences were universal. By the 80s, this was pretty well incorporated into feminist thought.

The problem with academic institution of feminism is that people outside academia were no longer thought of as the primary audience. Insights rarely reached many people. Depoliticization tended to undermine the movement as well. Effort must be made to reach people outside of academia. Without this, we risk losing the university programs too, because most of what people learn of feminism in the patriarchal mass media is negative. "The citizens of this nation cannot know the positive contributions feminist movement has made to all our lives if we do not highlight gains."
